📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can deduct only the medical and dental costs above 7.50% of your adjusted gross income, your income minus a few adjustments, and only if you itemize. Count the health premiums you pay yourself, Medicare’s included. If you’re self-employed and can’t join an employer’s blueprint, deduct your premiums separately, with no threshold or itemizing, up to your business’s profit.

According to recent reports, for a retiree with $60,000 of adjusted gross income, which is her income after a few adjustments, the 7.50% threshold is $4,500. With $9,000 of medical costs, Medicare premiums included, she can deduct the $4,500 above it if itemizing beats her standard deduction, which is bigger for anyone 65 or older.

Industry observers note that count what you paid out of pocket for doctors, hospitals, dentists, prescriptions, glasses, and hearing aids, plus the miles you drive to appointments at the IRS’s medical mileage rate. Premiums count too, including Medicare Part B and Part D, coverage you buy yourself, and qualified long-term care insurance up to an IRS limit set by age.

It has been revealed that nonprescription medicine other than insulin, most cosmetic surgery, and gym dues for general fitness don’t count. Neither do premiums your employer takes out of your pay before tax, or bills you pay from a health savings account, since that money was never taxed. IRS Publication 502 lists the rest.

In a recent development, if you’re self-employed, premiums for health coverage you buy on your own go on Schedule 1 instead, where they lower your adjusted gross income without a threshold or itemizing. Medicare premiums count there too, but the deduction can’t exceed your business’s profit. Any month you could join a subsidized proposal through your job or your spouse’s doesn’t qualify, and premiums the deduction doesn’t cover can count with your other medical costs.

In a recent development, costs count in the year you pay them, and a credit card charge counts in the year you make it, even if you pay off the card later. Say the retiree’s income stays at $60,000 and her costs run $6,000 a year. That clears her $4,500 threshold by $1,500 each year, or $3,000 over two years. The same $12,000 paid in one year clears it by $7,500, and that larger total is likelier to beat her standard deduction.

Once this year’s costs get close to your threshold, have the dental work, hearing aids, or eye surgery you’ve been putting off done before December 31, and pay the bill by then.

Breaking: What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

📅 07 May 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone.
  • According to recent reports, dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table.
  • In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

According to recent reports, dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

It has been revealed that dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

The result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

According to recent reports, most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

In a recent development, the mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

Because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

In a recent development, for most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

Say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:.

Recent findings suggest that after three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

This is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

It removes emotion from investing.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

It makes market downturns work for you.

When markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

It is accessible no matter your income.

You do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

Sources indicate that consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

Want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

It has been revealed that if you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single firm’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small.

Industry observers note that things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market.

Sources indicate that research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That noted, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:.

According to recent reports, dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

Sources indicate that the key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

What Are Mutual Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list.
  • This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.
  • In a recent development, A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

In a recent development, A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

According to recent reports, each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Sources indicate that mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

When you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it looks to do it.

Investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund manufacturer or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

Recent findings suggest that these funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds (fixed income funds).

It has been revealed that bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

These funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Industry observers note that index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most key things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

Sources indicate that an actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

According to recent reports, the problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

Sources indicate that for most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Recent findings suggest that fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

In a recent development, the expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

It has been revealed that some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

In a recent development, these are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

When you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

For investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

It has been revealed that most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly.

It has been revealed that this is the biggest issue with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Industry observers note that because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

When a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an issue in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

It is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

Recent findings suggest that with thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

In a recent development, that noted, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most key step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Invoice factoring turns your unpaid invoices into cash within days, but the factoring company keeps 1% to 5% of each invoice for every 30 days it goes unpaid.
  • A trucking, staffing, manufacturing, or wholesale business can finish a job and wait 30 to 90 days to get paid, while the bills for the next job come due now.
  • With factoring, you sell the unpaid invoice to a factoring company, or factor, which typically advances you 70% to 90% of its value within days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Invoice factoring turns your unpaid invoices into cash within days, but the factoring company keeps 1% to 5% of each invoice for every 30 days it goes unpaid. Factor only when waiting would cost you more than that fee, and pick non-recourse factoring if one customer going broke would sink your business.

A trucking, staffing, manufacturing, or wholesale business can finish a job and wait 30 to 90 days to get paid, while the bills for the next job come due now.

With factoring, you sell the unpaid invoice to a factoring company, or factor, which typically advances you 70% to 90% of its value within days. The factor collects from your customer and sends you the rest, minus its fee. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce puts that fee at 1% to 5% of the invoice for every 30 days it stays unpaid.

Say a trucking company factors $80,000 in invoices due in 45 days, with a 90% advance and a 3% fee. It gets $72,000 now and the last $8,000, minus the $2,400 fee, when its customers pay. That $2,400 is the same cost as borrowing the $72,000 for 45 days at roughly 27% a year.

It has been revealed that the fee is worth paying only when the cash earns more than $2,400 in those 45 days, such as by funding loads the company would otherwise turn down. If the $72,000 would sit in the bank until its customers pay, the $2,400 is wasted.

A bank line of credit usually costs less than factoring, so get a quote on one first if your business qualifies. Factoring fits when you can’t get one or your sales have outgrown your credit limit, since the factor looks mostly at your customers’ credit.

In a recent development, recourse factoring costs less than non-recourse, but you repay the factor when a customer never pays. Non-recourse shifts that loss to the factor, so buy it if one big customer going broke would sink you. It usually covers only a customer that goes broke, not one that disputes the bill.

Before you sign, check the contract for a monthly minimum you must factor, a term of up to two years, and a fee to leave early. Then get the fees for invoices paid in 30, 60, and 90 days in writing, since a fee charged every 30 days triples when a customer takes 90 days to pay.

How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,.

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

According to recent reports, okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

In a recent development, so I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

Industry observers note that I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

It has been revealed that I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

It has been revealed that then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

According to recent reports, during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

According to recent reports, but eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

Recent findings suggest that it reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning newly introduced things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

Industry observers note that so I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

According to recent reports, thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

In a recent development, as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An early-payment discount is an expensive way to get paid sooner.
  • On a $10,000 invoice, 2/10 net 30 means collecting $9,800 on day 10 instead of $10,000 on day 30.
  • Industry observers note that as an annual interest rate, that’s $200 ÷ $9,800 × 365 ÷ 20, or about 37%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An early-payment discount is an expensive way to get paid sooner. Offering 2/10 net 30, 2% off for paying in 10 days instead of 30, costs you the equivalent of about 37% a year in interest. Offer one only when you need the cash and borrowing it would cost you more.

On a $10,000 invoice, 2/10 net 30 means collecting $9,800 on day 10 instead of $10,000 on day 30. You give up $200 to get your money 20 days sooner.

Industry observers note that as an annual interest rate, that’s $200 ÷ $9,800 × 365 ÷ 20, or about 37%. To check any other offer, divide what you give up by the cash you get early, then multiply by 365 divided by the number of days early.

In the October survey by the National Federation of Independent Business, small business owners paid an average interest rate of 8.5% on loans of a year or less. At about 37%, 2/10 net 30 costs more than four times that 8.5%, so a line of credit near that rate is the cheaper way to cover a short cash gap. The same formula works on a factoring firm’s offer to buy your unpaid invoices.

According to recent reports, before you discount anything, send each invoice the day the work is done, which costs nothing. The discount is worth its price in a cash crunch, when a large unpaid invoice would leave you unable to make payroll and you can’t borrow the difference. With a customer who usually pays on day 50, the discount brings the money in 40 days early instead of 20, and its cost drops from about 37% a year to about 19%.

In a recent development, offer it only to the customers whose early payment you need. A printing company with no credit line, short of cash in its slow quarter, offers 1/10 net 30 to just its three largest accounts. They usually pay on day 30, so the printer collects $60,000 of invoices 20 days sooner for $600, about 18% a year, and everyone else still pays in full.

Recent findings suggest that write the deadline as a date and both amounts in dollars. On a $5,000 invoice dated March 2, that’s “2% discount ($100) for payment received by March 12. Full $5,000 due April 1.” The word “received” means a check mailed on March 12 doesn’t count. Bill the $100 to any customer who takes the discount after March 12.

For a line of credit to draw on instead of offering a discount, compare the best small business loans.

Sell on Fiverr if your service can be packaged at a set price, like logo design or voiceovers, because buyers search for it and order without a pitch from you. Fiverr keeps 20% of every order, tips included, so build that cut into each package’s price.

It has been revealed that fiverr is a freelance marketplace where you sell your skills as packaged services, called gigs, at prices you set. On a $100 order, you keep $80 after Fiverr’s 20% cut and pay no Fiverr fee to withdraw it to PayPal, so price a package at $125 to net $100.

Freelancers with a service they can package and price up front, such as logo design, editing, or voiceovers, get a storefront that buyers already search, and that’s worth the 20% cut. A consultant whose work needs a custom quote does better on Upwork, where freelancers send proposals to the jobs clients post.

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • According to recent reports, but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

According to recent reports, but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

Industry observers note that but a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

According to recent reports, yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health firm that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Recent findings suggest that long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

In a recent development, another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new firm, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

It has been revealed that and wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

In a recent development, this is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

But there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

It has been revealed that while this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

It has been revealed that and while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

Industry observers note that so I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

It has been revealed that but on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Sources indicate that many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

In a recent development, since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a newly introduced, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the concern, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

According to recent reports, many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

Sources indicate that more modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

According to recent reports, and it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

It has been revealed that the great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Industry observers note that note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

Gifting Your House Costs Your Family the Tax Break They’d Get by Inheriting It

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (376 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giving your house to a child or grandchild while you’re alive hands them your cost basis, the figure their capital gain is measured from, so selling it can cost them tax on years of growth.
  • Signing the house over to family looks simple, until they sell.
  • Recent findings suggest that your cost basis is what you paid for the house plus improvements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giving your house to a child or grandchild while you’re alive hands them your cost basis, the figure their capital gain is measured from, so selling it can cost them tax on years of growth. If its value has climbed, leave it to them instead, since an heir who sells owes tax only on growth after your death.

Signing the house over to family looks simple, until they sell.

Recent findings suggest that your cost basis is what you paid for the house plus improvements. Say a mother paid $90,000 for her house and gives it to her son, who sells it at today’s $490,000 value. He takes her $90,000 basis, so the sale leaves him a $400,000 taxable gain. If he owns and lives in it two of the five years before selling, the home sale tax exclusion shelters up to $250,000 of it ($500,000 on a joint return). She’d also file a gift tax return, but owe gift tax only after using up a lifetime exemption in the millions.

If he inherits it at that value instead, his basis steps up to $490,000, and he owes nothing on the sale.

So if your house has gained value, leave it at your death through a will, a living trust you can change, or a transfer-on-death deed where your state allows one. If it must change hands sooner, sell it at market value, lending the buyer the money through seller financing if needed, so their basis is the price paid. Or give only part of it, and the share you keep steps up at your death.

A gift during your life carries other costs too:.

Before anyone signs a deed, have an estate planning attorney in your state draw it up.

Interest-Free Credit From Suppliers – Ask for Longer Terms and Pay on the Due Date

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (498 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Supplier payment terms are credit that charges no interest, and every extra day you get keeps cash in your business.
  • Paying suppliers on delivery, or paying each invoice the day it arrives, hands over cash that terms would let you keep for weeks.
  • Industry observers note that terms like net 30 give you 30 days after the invoice date to pay the full bill, with no interest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Supplier payment terms are credit that charges no interest, and every extra day you get keeps cash in your business. Once you’ve paid a supplier on time for a few months, ask for 30 to 60 days to pay. Then pay each bill on its due date, not early, unless the supplier offers a discount for paying sooner.

Paying suppliers on delivery, or paying each invoice the day it arrives, hands over cash that terms would let you keep for weeks. That cash could be covering payroll, rent, or the next order.

Industry observers note that terms like net 30 give you 30 days after the invoice date to pay the full bill, with no interest. Take a gift shop that buys about $12,000 a month from its two biggest suppliers and pays on delivery. Moving both to net 45 means it pays for each order a month and a half later, so about $18,000 more stays in its account going into the holiday season.

It has been revealed that ask for longer terms after a few months of paying a supplier on time, since that record is your best argument. Go from paying on delivery to net 30, or from net 30 to net 45 or net 60. Better still, ask for terms that match how long your own customers take to pay you, so their payments come in by the time your bills come due.

In a recent development, then pay on the due date, not before and never after, with each payment scheduled in your bank’s bill pay to arrive that day. Many suppliers report how you pay to Dun & Bradstreet, whose PAYDEX business credit score tracks how promptly you pay them. A late payment can pull that score down, and it gives a supplier reason to shorten your terms, not lengthen them.

The exception is a discount for paying early. Terms of 2/10 net 30 take 2% off a bill paid within 10 days and otherwise give you 30 days to pay it in full. Saving 2% for paying 20 days sooner is like earning about 37% a year on that money, far more than a savings account pays, so take the discount whenever you have the cash to spare. Offering your own customers an early-payment discount turns that 37% into a cost you pay.

Start with the supplier you pay the most, since every extra 30 days of terms keeps about one month’s worth of its bills in your account.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you can afford a loved one’s bail, pay it in full to the court. The money comes back when the case ends, as long as they make every court date, minus any fees or fines the court deducts. A bail bondsman’s fee, usually 10% of the bail, is gone even if the charges are dropped.

Sources indicate that say a judge sets $5,000 bail, the charges are later dismissed, and the court deducts nothing. A mother who paid her son’s bail in cash gets all $5,000 back, while a neighbor who paid a bondsman the usual 10% fee on the same amount is out $500 for good.

According to recent reports, the court holds the cash until the case is over, which can take months, and some courts keep part of it. New York keeps 3% of it after a conviction, and Florida first withholds any unpaid court costs and fines the defendant owes. Even that 3% is less than a third of a bondsman’s usual 10% fee.

A bondsman gives the court a written promise to pay the full bail if the defendant misses court, and the fee pays for that promise. Whoever pays the fee usually signs as the cosigner, on the hook for that full amount, so the fee isn’t the most you can lose. The bondsman may also hold collateral against that debt, such as your car’s title or a lien on your house.

Industry observers note that illinois, Kentucky, Oregon, and Wisconsin ban bail bondsmen, and Illinois ended cash bail entirely in 2023. Wherever a judge sets bail, take these steps:.

Whichever you choose, put every court date on your calendar and get the defendant to each one. One missed date can cost you the full bail.

Renting to Section 8 Tenants Means Steady Rent – With Inspections, Rent Reviews & Paperwork

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (495 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With a Section 8 tenant, the local housing authority pays its share of the rent straight to you, but only for a unit that passes its inspection at a rent it approves.
  • HUD’s fact sheet for landlords promises timely payments and claims voucher tenants stay in a unit seven to eight years on average.
  • The tenant usually pays 30% of their income after deductions toward rent and utilities, and the authority pays the rest, up to its payment standard, the most it pays for a unit that size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With a Section 8 tenant, the local housing authority pays its share of the rent straight to you, but only for a unit that passes its inspection at a rent it approves. Check your state and local law before you decide, since many states and cities bar turning down an applicant for paying with a voucher.

HUD’s fact sheet for landlords promises timely payments and claims voucher tenants stay in a unit seven to eight years on average.

The tenant usually pays 30% of their income after deductions toward rent and utilities, and the authority pays the rest, up to its payment standard, the most it pays for a unit that size. The tenant pays any rent above the standard, but at move-in their share can’t top 40% of their income after deductions.

Take a tenant with no deductions, in a unit whose rent includes utilities and falls within the standard. Earning $24,000 a year, they pay 30% of $2,000 a month, or $600, and on a $1,600 rent the authority sends you the other $1,000.

According to recent reports, before payments start, you sign a contract with the authority, add HUD’s tenancy addendum to your lease, and pass its inspection. A failed item means repairs and a recheck, often while the unit sits empty. Inspectors return at least every two years, or every three at a small rural authority. They use HUD’s Housing Quality Standards or the newer NSPIRE standard, which a July 2026 HUD notice tells every authority to adopt by Feb. 1, 2027.

According to recent reports, the authority also limits your rent to what similar unsubsidized units rent for. The addendum bars an increase during the lease’s first term and requires 60 days’ notice to the authority before a later one, which it checks against similar units too. So the program suits a unit that’s already in good repair and priced near local market rents.

It has been revealed that the authority’s payments depend on federal funding, which can run late. After the 2025 government shutdown, Georgia’s Department of Community Affairs didn’t pay landlords the rest of November’s housing assistance until Dec. 5. Under the addendum, you can’t charge the tenant the authority’s share or evict them over its late payment.

The Poverty & Race Research Action Council lists the state and local laws that protect voucher holders. Where one covers your rental, screen voucher holders by the same written standard you use for every applicant.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, spend your first day at a upcoming job meeting people, not hunting for documents. The night before, gather your bank details for direct deposit and the documents that prove you can work in the U.S. Once you’re there, ask your manager what success looks like in your first 90 days.

Expect three forms by day one, and each needs something only you can supply. One proves you can work in the U.S., one sets up direct deposit, and the third, a W-4, sets how much federal income tax comes out of each paycheck.

The first, Form I-9, has a deadline. Your employer has three business days from your first day to examine your documents, and it may let you go if they’re missing. A U.S. passport is enough on its own. Otherwise, pair an ID such as a driver’s license with your Social Security card or birth certificate, or pick another pair from the list of acceptable documents. Bring originals that haven’t expired, since photocopies don’t count. For a lost one, bring the receipt showing you’ve applied to replace it.

Then settle the rest the night before:.

A upcoming hire who brings her passport and a voided check can finish the paperwork in ten minutes and spend the rest of the morning meeting the team.

Sources indicate that on day one, arrive a few minutes early, write down names as you meet people, and take notes on how work gets done. Then ask your manager what success looks like in your first 90 days.

You don’t have to pick your benefits on day one, but the window to enroll is often 30 days from your start. Missing it usually means waiting for open enrollment, which comes once a year at most employers. Find your deadline and put it on your calendar before you leave.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (456 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Family or Friend Won’t Repay a Loan? Get a Payment Plan in Writing First

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If a relative or friend has stopped repaying money you lent them, ask privately for a payment blueprint they can afford, with a set amount and start date.
  • Without a set payment or due date, repaying a loan is easy to put off, and every month of silence makes the subject harder to raise.
  • So skip the hints and make one specific request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If a relative or friend has stopped repaying money you lent them, ask privately for a payment blueprint they can afford, with a set amount and start date. Confirm it in a text they answer. Save a demand letter or small claims court for a broken plan, or forgive the rest and say so.

Without a set payment or due date, repaying a loan is easy to put off, and every month of silence makes the subject harder to raise.

So skip the hints and make one specific request. Call or meet in private. A text is easy to ignore, and with others listening, embarrassment can turn into an argument. Propose an amount and a schedule they can actually meet. A sister owed $2,400 might ask her brother for $100 a month starting next payday, which clears the debt in two years.

Afterward, text them a short summary of the plan and ask them to confirm it. Their reply is a written record that they owe the money and agreed to repay it, which matters if the plan falls apart.

Sources indicate that if payments don’t start, or start and then stop, put the request in writing. Send a short letter or email that states what they owe, the payments they missed, a deadline to pay, and that you’ll file in small claims court if they don’t. Keep a copy. California’s courts require you to ask for the money before you file, and your copy indicates the judge you did.

Sources indicate that once the deadline passes, file in small claims court. It takes claims up to a cap your state sets, from $2,500 in Kentucky to $25,000 in Delaware and Tennessee. Filing is cheap. California’s fee for a $2,400 claim is $50. For the hearing, bring the bank or payment app record of the transfer and every message in which they agreed to repay you.

Suing a relative or friend can cost you the relationship, win or lose. When the relationship matters more than the money, forgive the rest on purpose and tell them it’s now a gift, which settles the debt for both of you. Then stop lending to that person. For anyone else, lend only money you could afford to give away.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That noted, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like latest credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most crucial concerns for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

According to recent reports, generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

According to recent reports, most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

It has been revealed that one step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you initiative to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Sources indicate that your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit swiftly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

Sources indicate that while secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

It has been revealed that in fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

Sources indicate that there are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an problem with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

It has been revealed that college students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (493 w)

Tech Report: Cash Is King for Small Businesses – Keep Three Months of Fixed Costs in Reserve

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that keep a cash reserve worth at least three months of your business’s fixed costs, the bills that don’t shrink when sales do.
  • In a recent development, in 2025, the typical small business with a Chase business account had cash to cover less than 18 days of its usual spending if no money came in, the JPMorganChase Institute found.
  • Size the reserve by fixed costs, not total spending.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that keep a cash reserve worth at least three months of your business’s fixed costs, the bills that don’t shrink when sales do. Hold it in a separate business savings account that pays interest, so a slow season or a customer who pays late doesn’t force you into costly borrowing.

In a recent development, in 2025, the typical small business with a Chase business account had cash to cover less than 18 days of its usual spending if no money came in, the JPMorganChase Institute found. With that little cash, one big customer paying a few weeks late can leave you short for payroll.

Size the reserve by fixed costs, not total spending. When sales slow, you buy less inventory, but rent, insurance, loan payments, subscriptions, and the pay of the staff you keep come due in full. If your sales are seasonal, hold three months of those bills plus the part of them your slow-season sales don’t cover, since that gap returns every year.

To build it, pick a share of a typical month’s profit and set up a recurring transfer of that amount into a separate business savings or money market account that pays interest. Kept out of checking, the reserve won’t get spent on everyday bills, and it stays apart from your household emergency fund, which covers your own bills if the business can’t pay you.

In a recent development, say a dental practice’s rent, staff pay, equipment loan payment, and insurance come to $45,000 a month. Its three-month reserve is $135,000, built over two years at $5,625 a month. When an insurer holds up the practice’s claim payments for six weeks, the practice covers payroll from the reserve instead of borrowing, then refills it as the payments arrive.

According to recent reports, spend the reserve only on a real shortfall, such as a late payment, a slow season, or a broken machine you can’t work without, never on an opportunity like a bulk discount. Refill it from the next money that comes in, before you spend on anything that can wait. With a 13-week cash forecast, you can see a shortfall weeks before it hits. A business line of credit, opened while sales are strong, can cover a gap that outlasts the reserve.

Recent findings suggest that pull last year’s bank statements, total the fixed costs, and divide by four for your three-month target. Then set up the recurring transfer before this month ends.
